stops.name: San Martín de los Andes, Lake Lácar and the vocation
stops.campa: The road climbs into the lake country and stops the travelers' breath: Lácar lying dark blue between forested walls, the Andes closing the sky. They camp, roast stolen-cheap lamb, and are offered a future: a local caretaker's dream of a clinic on the lakeshore, a settled life in paradise. That night by the water both men look at the offered happiness and refuse it, and in the refusal discover what they actually are. The diary records the vow of the wanderers; the lake keeps the oath.
stops.quote: Then we understood that our vocation, our true vocation, was to roam forever along the roads and seas of the world.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries

stops.name: San Carlos de Bariloche, Chichina's letter
stops.campa: Along the Seven Lakes road the Norton limps into Bariloche, and in the poste restante a letter from Chichina waits like a document of severance: it is over. Ernesto reads it in the shelter's kitchen light and something closes quietly. He had carried her bracelet as an amulet; now the last anchor to the life of the Córdoba salons is cut by the woman herself. The diary is laconic and wounded. Outside, Nahuel Huapi lies under storm light, and across the water is Chile: the road forward, which is now the only direction he owns.

stops.name: Lakes crossing to Peulla, into Chile over Frías
stops.campa: The frontier is crossed by water, in the old ceremonial way: the Modesta Victoria across Nahuel Huapi, the green mirror of Laguna Frías, La Poderosa lashed to the deck like a sarcophagus, and finally Peulla on the Chilean side, under the white cone of Tronador. Customs men eye the overloaded bike and the two threadbare 'doctors'. Argentina drops behind with Chichina's letter still fresh; Chile opens ahead as the first foreign country of the myth, lake-cold and volcano-lit. The continent begins here.

stops.name: Temuco, 'two Argentine experts in leprology'
stops.campa: In Temuco the travelers perform their masterpiece of picaresque diplomacy: the newspaper El Austral publishes them under the headline 'Two Argentine experts in leprology travel South America by motorcycle,' and for a week the clipping is a passport that opens garages, dinner tables and wine cellars. Ernesto notes with amusement how a little printed importance transforms them from vagabonds into dignitaries. The Norton, less impressed by fame, is coming apart beneath them, shedding pieces of itself along the Chilean south.

stops.name: Lautaro, the dance, the chase, the dying Norton
stops.campa: At Lautaro the gearbox is welded and the town offers a dance. Ernesto, loose with Chilean wine, courts a mechanic's wife too openly on the dance floor and the evening ends with the two Argentines fleeing the hall under a hail of curses, pursued by indignant husbands and their friends. Days later, on the road toward Malleco, La Poderosa's frame gives way at last in a slow, terminal crash. The Mighty One's agony has begun: from here the motorcycle journey becomes a journey of walkers, stowaways and beggars, which is to say, its true self.

stops.name: Los Ángeles, death of La Poderosa
stops.campa: In Los Ángeles the verdict is pronounced: La Poderosa II will ride no more. The travelers sleep in the fire station among the volunteer firemen, and Ernesto joins a midnight run to a burning house, hauling hose in borrowed helmet: the asthmatic medical student as bombero for one night. The dead Norton is crated onto a truck for Santiago. Stripped of their machine, the two are now purely what the road makes them: cargo, guests, mendicants of Latin America. The diary notes the loss like the death of a comrade.

stops.name: Santiago de Chile, farewell to the machine
stops.campa: Santiago receives them on the back of the truck that carries the corpse of La Poderosa. In the capital they leave the motorcycle in a garage forever, gate-crash the hospitality of the Argentine consulate, and study the political fever of election-year Chile: Ibáñez posters, Allende posters, talk in every kitchen. Ernesto diagnoses the country in his notebook with the cold, affectionate eye that is becoming his instrument. Then, with nothing left to ride, the two point themselves north toward the desert on foot and by grace of passing trucks.

stops.name: Valparaíso, La Gioconda and the dying woman
stops.campa: In the vertical port city, all stairways and funiculars and ship smoke, the owner of the café La Gioconda feeds the penniless travelers on credit and philosophy. Ernesto is called to a shack on the hills to see an old woman dying of asthma and heart failure amid poverty with nothing to prescribe. Standing uselessly at her bed, the young doctor has the vision that reorders his life: medicine cannot cure what an unjust order inflicts. The diary entry he writes that night is the first page of the revolutionary he will become.
stops.quote: There, in the final moments of people whose farthest horizon has always been tomorrow, one grasps the profound tragedy that circumscribes the life of the proletariat the whole world over.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries, Valparaíso chapter

stops.name: Stowaways on the San Antonio: Valparaíso to Antofagasta
stops.campa: Denied passage to Easter Island and short of everything, the two smuggle themselves aboard the freighter San Antonio in the night, hiding in a latrine among the smell of the sea's injustice. Discovered at sea, they are hauled before an amused captain and sentenced to work: Alberto peels potatoes, Ernesto scrubs the famous latrine. On deck at night, wind over the black Pacific, the stowaway watches the coast of the great desert north slide by and feels the joy of the trick: the continent crossed by cunning when money fails.

stops.name: Baquedano, the communist couple in the desert night
stops.campa: In the freezing dark of the Atacama, at the rail junction of Baquedano, the travelers share a candle and a blanketless night with a mining couple: communists, hounded, the man just out of prison, both walking toward the sulphur mines where no one asks your politics because the work kills you regardless. They have not one blanket between them. Ernesto gives them his and lies awake in the cold. In the couple's silent dignity he sees, he writes, the living portrait of the proletariat of the whole world, and the night enters the canon as a conversion scene.
stops.quote: It was one of the coldest nights of my life, but one which made me feel a little closer to this strange, for me, human species.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries, Baquedano chapter

stops.name: Chuquicamata, the copper mountain
stops.campa: They stand at the lip of the largest open-pit copper mine on earth, an amphitheater of terraces gnawed into the Andes by American machinery, and watch the wealth of Chile ride conveyor belts toward other people's futures. The blond, efficient managers of the Yankee company tolerate the visitors without warmth; the miners' graveyard tolerates everyone. Ernesto counts the dead in silicosis and the profit in dollars and writes the arithmetic into his notebook. Chuquicamata is the journey's great industrial vision: the mountain eaten alive, and the verdict forming.
stops.quote: The greatest effort Chile must make is to shake its uncomfortable Yankee friend from its back.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries, Chuquicamata chapter

stops.name: Tarata, the defeated race
stops.campa: Crossing into Peru at Tacna and climbing by truck into the altiplano, the travelers reach the stone village of Tarata, where Aymara families ride the truck-beds with their animals and their silence. Ernesto looks at faces that once belonged to an empire and sees four centuries of defeat administered like a slow medicine. The diary entry he writes here is the harshest and most pitying of the journey: the Indian world is not picturesque to him, it is a crime scene. The mountains hold the cold; the notebook holds the indictment.
stops.quote: The people before us are not the same proud race that time and again rose up against Inca rule... these are a defeated race.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries, Tarata chapter
